consensus_summary: Consensus primary reading treats 'rich' as material wealth producing self-sufficiency, misplaced trust in possessions, and spiritual peril/obstacle to the kingdom (with Rev 3:17 as key ironic proof); common alternatives are spiritual riches in faith/grace, OT blessing, oppression class, or neutral stewardship.
book_summary: Rich = the self-sufficient who believe they need nothing and therefore cannot receive; true wealth = riches toward God as tested faith and righteous covering. Opposite: Poor.
consensus_core_identification: materially wealthy persons whose abundance fosters self-sufficiency and spiritual danger/misplaced trust
book_core_identification: the self-sufficient who believe they need nothing and therefore cannot receive
boundary_disagreement: Book tightens the referent to the precise attitude of needlessness that blocks reception and defines true riches strictly as tested faith + righteous covering, thereby excluding or demoting consensus cases of OT blessing-prosperity, pure socioeconomic class, oppression typology, and broader 'riches of grace' language as the primary sense.
rationale: Both center on self-sufficiency drawn from the same Laodicean and Lukan texts; the book preserves that category but narrows its extension and precision to those who 'cannot receive' while adding a tightly specified positive counterpart, producing boundary refinement rather than core replacement or novelty.
strongest_objection: Some consensus strands (esp. B) elevate spiritual wealth itself as the primary symbolic meaning, so the book's exclusive foregrounding of the negative self-sufficient posture could be seen as selective.
